analysis.title: Third Quarter 2026 Investor Letter
key_insights: Third Point flagship Offshore Fund returned -6.8% net in Q3 2026 (YTD -0.1%, annualized 12.8% since Dec 1996), against the CS HF Event-Driven Index at -1.0% and the S&P 500 TR at +2.3%. The New Series, which excludes legacy private investments, returned -8.6% in Q3 and -2.0% YTD.

Index performance was benign but factors were not. The Morgan Stanley TMT Momentum factor fell more than 50% from its late-June peak to mid-August, its largest drawdown since inception. The broad momentum factor had its highest volatility in 45 years. The Goldman Sachs High-Beta Momentum basket has had 39 one-day moves above 5% this year, the most since 1999 outside 2020 (41).

Drivers of the Q3 drawdown: focus on AI capex and its funding, open-source models, slowing growth at frontier labs, and crowding and leverage (the unwind at Situational Awareness, retail liquidation of leveraged memory-stock ETFs in Korea). SK Hynix, Flex and MasTec, which drove Q2 returns, were caught in the rout.

Oil and rates: the June ceasefire with Iran collapsed in early July, the Strait of Hormuz closed, and the US blockade of Iranian ports plus tanker attacks took Brent from about $72 on July 1 to a $109 peak by mid-September. Headline CPI re-accelerated to 3.7% and Fed Chair Kevin Warsh raised the funds rate to 3.75-4.00%, the first hike since 2023.

The 10-year yield is above 5% with the economy still growing. The letter attributes part of this to inflation expectations after five years of stacked supply shocks and part to supply: AI-capex borrowers compete with sovereigns for the same bond buyers.

Bull side of the tug of war: S&P 500 Q3 earnings tracking close to 30% growth (third straight quarter above 25%), AI usage holding up, and the Muse launch and growth metrics in Anthropic's S-1. Bear side: 10-year above 5%, unresolved Middle East conflict, high oil, and less willingness to treat AI as a single investment theme.

The AI debate has moved from whether demand is real to whether the capital can be funded and earn a return. Consensus has hyperscalers and frontier labs spending $5-7 trillion over 2025-2030. At a low-teens hurdle, that needs $2-3 trillion of incremental annual AI revenue, against about $6 trillion of global IT spend today.

Credit is showing the strain: some data-center financings in high yield and leveraged loans yield double digits, top-rated data-center ABS that priced below 5% in January yields near 7%, and CDS on Oracle, Meta and Nvidia hit records in late October. Some banks and insurers are nearing exposure limits, and neocloud financing depends on backstops from hyperscalers and chipmakers.

Reasons the letter gives for believing projected AI spending is overstated and will be stretched over more years: AI addresses markets larger than IT spend (up to a $60 trillion knowledge-worker TAM), cloud revenue is accelerating with backlogs growing at triple-digit rates, the two leading frontier labs generate over $100 billion in combined run-rate revenue, and hyperscalers say servers pay back in under three years. Open-source models are within six months of the frontier, so who captures the economics matters more than in June.

Middle East base case is a muddle-through stalemate with oil elevated and the economy slowing without breaking. Tail risk is damage to Gulf infrastructure. The letter calls a deal after November 3 the underappreciated path, and sees the midterms as a clearing event for political uncertainty.

The letter sees signs of excess in private markets: $1 billion-plus valuations for pre-revenue seed companies, allocation frenzy for growth-stage names, and SPVs selling private-deal access at high fees. It expects lower multiples given market fragility, citing ServiceNow, Intel and Reddit each losing about a third of market cap in one day last week.

Positioning: gross and net exposure are significantly lower. Third Point cut semiconductor, data-center-adjacent and hyperscaler positions, and added financials, live events, industrials, commercial aerospace and consumer names. Gross short exposure is about 21% of NAV, all single-name, with themes in GLP-1 losers, cable, P&C insurance and housing. Shorts on AI disruptees (software, information services, IT services) were reduced because they amplified the AI longs and created basis risk.

The index trades at about 20x forward earnings on roughly 30% earnings growth, and the firm does not want risk there. It is willing to miss an early rally to preserve capital and sees a possible environment like March 2020 or the late GFC, where the next opportunities come from credit.

Atom Computing, a private legacy position, was the top Q3 winner. Third Point led the Series B (late 2021) and Series C (early 2026). The Series D-1 closed in July 2026 at a stepped-up valuation, and a Series D-2 from a major sector investor will close in coming weeks at a meaningfully higher valuation, over 28x the entry valuation. Atom received a $100 million CHIPS Act investment (May 2026) and a DARPA QBI Stage C award worth up to $300 million contingent on milestones.

APi Group long thesis: more than half of revenue is recurring inspection, service and monitoring. Each dollar of inspection revenue generates $3-4 of annual service work, and North American inspection revenue has grown at a high single digit rate or better for 25 straight quarters. Management targets a 2028 adjusted EBITDA margin of at least 16% and over 60% recurring mix. Pro forma net leverage is 2.4x and the stock trades about 18x Third Point's FY28 EPS.

Corporate credit gave back its Q2 gains. Shorts in telecom, building products and healthcare gained, and Bausch Health rose on solid operations and a favorable patent ruling. The largest single detractor was the GSE preferreds, where the market implies only a 15% probability of an IPO, which Third Point calls too low. AI infrastructure positions were the largest detractors overall.

AI infrastructure credit: Goldman Sachs expects hyperscaler debt issuance to rise about 60% YoY in 2027 to over $400 billion, and about $300 billion of global project finance issuance, up 2-2.5x. Hyperscaler 10-year spreads are +50bps YTD and HY project finance bonds are about 250bps wider since the June tights. Third Point sees the near-term path of least resistance as lower for these securities and compares market treatment to 'death spiral preferreds'.

Third Point prefers hyperscalers and certain project finance structures for AI exposure and does not expect issuance to change hyperscaler cost of capital materially. It unwound nearly all equity shorts that hedged its infrastructure credit and still finds relative-value shorts in BB-rated data center bonds. It made a convertible loan to neocloud Nscale, citing debt downside protection, equity upside, Nvidia guarantees and a conversion struck at a discount to the IPO level.

Structured credit was about flat in Q3. Third Point is constructive on residential mortgage securities (bought BBB at an 8.5% yield, versus a high 6% a few weeks earlier, and sees opportunities above 10% over six weeks), leveraged loans and CLOs (spreads widening, LME maturity walls in 2027-2028), and consumer ABS (subprime pressure, student loan 2023-2025 vintages likely to take losses, rising subprime auto delinquencies). It expects a more pronounced credit cycle next year.

market_movers.rationale: Third Point profiles APi Group as a long-term compounder with recurring inspection revenue and a multi-year runway for double-digit EPS growth. The stock trades about 18x its FY28 EPS.
Bausch Health was a top-five Q3 winner on solid operating results and a favorable patent ruling.
Meta was a top-five Q3 winner for the fund. The letter also notes Meta's possible sale of excess compute capacity was read as an overbuilding signal and that Meta CDS hit a record in late October.
Warner Bros Discovery was a top-five Q3 winner.
SK Hynix was the largest Q3 loser, hit by the memory-stock rout and leveraged ETF liquidation in Korea.
Flex was a top-five Q3 loser after driving Q2 returns.

CRH was a top-five Q3 loser.
TTM Technologies was a top-five Q3 loser.

Consumer credit deterioration, with subprime auto delinquencies rising and student loan ABS impairment.
Leveraged loan LME maturity walls in 2027 and 2028.
Dependence of the market on successful IPOs and continued growth of two frontier model companies.

The US blockade of Iranian ports and attacks on tankers pushed Brent to $109 by mid-September.
